segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they came to the tomb, bringing the spices they had prepared.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They found the stone rolled away from the tomb,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but when they went in they did not find the body.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While they were at a loss about this, suddenly two men in dazzling clothing stood beside them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The women were terrified and bowed their faces to the ground, but the men said to them,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Why are you looking for the living one among the dead?

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: He is not here; he has been raised. Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: that the Son of Man must be handed over into the hands of sinful people, and be crucified, and on the third day rise.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they remembered his words,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and returning from the tomb they reported all these things to the eleven and to all the rest.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The women were Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and the others with them; they kept telling the apostles these things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But to them these words seemed like nonsense, and they did not believe the women.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter, however, got up and ran to the tomb. Stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths and nothing else, and he went home, marveling at what had happened.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now on that same day two of them were on their way to a village named Emmaus, sixty stadia from Jerusalem,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they were talking with each other about all these things that had happened.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While they were talking and debating, Jesus himself came near and began walking with them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but their eyes were kept from recognizing him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What are these words you are exchanging with each other as you walk?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they stood still, their faces downcast.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One of them, named Cleopas, answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know what has happened there in these days?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What things?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The things about Jesus the Nazarene, who was a prophet, powerful in deed and word before God and all the people,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and how our chief priests and rulers handed him over to be condemned to death, and crucified him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But we were hoping that he was the one who was going to set Israel free. And yet, on top of all this, it is now the third day since these things happened.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Moreover, some women of our group astounded us. They were at the tomb early in the morning

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and, not finding his body, they came saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who say that he is alive.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Some of those with us went off to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “How foolish you are, and how slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Was it not necessary for the Messiah to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he explained to them the things about himself in all the Scriptures.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They drew near the village to which they were going, and he acted as though he were going farther.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they pressed him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Stay with us, for it is nearly evening and the day is already far gone.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he went in to stay with them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had reclined at the table with them, he took the bread and said the blessing, then broke it and began handing it to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then their eyes were opened and they recognized him, and he vanished from their sight.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to each other,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Were not our hearts burning within us as he spoke to us on the road, as he opened the Scriptures to us?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They got up that very hour and returned to Jerusalem, and they found the eleven and those with them gathered together,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who were saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The Lord really has been raised, and has appeared to Simon!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they themselves related what had happened on the road, and how he was made known to them in the breaking of the bread.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While they were saying these things, he himself stood among them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Startled and terrified, they thought they were seeing a ghost.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you troubled, and why are doubts rising in your hearts?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me and see, for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: [And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.]

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While they still could not believe it for joy and were marveling, he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do you have anything here to eat?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They handed him a piece of broiled fish,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he took it and ate it in front of them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you: everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “So it is written: the Messiah is to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and turning back and forgiveness of sins are to be proclaimed in his name to all the nations, beginning from Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You are witnesses of these things.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And look, I am sending upon you what my Father promised. But you, stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was blessing them, he parted from them [and was carried up into heaven].

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they [worshiped him and] returned to Jerusalem with great joy,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they were continually in the temple, blessing God.

notes.note: The Greek verb is passive in form and can mean either ‘he was raised’ (by God) or simply ‘he rose’. The passive is chosen here and in verse 34 because Luke elsewhere speaks of God raising Jesus, but many translations render it ‘he has risen’, and the grammar does not settle the question.

The Greek phrase ‘to himself’ can go with ‘went away’ (to his own place, that is, home) or with ‘marveling’ (wondering to himself). Most modern translations take it as ‘went home’. The whole verse is absent from a small group of ‘Western’ manuscripts, but it is present in the great majority, including the earliest.
A stadion was a Greek measure of roughly 185 metres, so sixty stadia is about eleven kilometres or seven miles, a walk of two to three hours. The location of Emmaus is disputed.

The verb means to release by payment or, more broadly, to liberate; the Greek Old Testament uses it for God bringing Israel out of Egypt. ‘Redeem’ is the traditional rendering and is accurate, but it now suggests personal salvation from sin, whereas the speakers are describing their hope for the nation's deliverance. Most translations keep ‘redeem’.

The Greek christos, ‘anointed one’, is here a title for the king Israel expected and not a name, and the point at issue is what that figure had to undergo. ‘Messiah’ makes the title audible; ‘Christ’ is kept in this translation where the word functions as a name. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

The Greek has no object: ‘he blessed’. At a Jewish meal the blessing over bread was a short prayer of praise addressed to God, not a consecration of the food, so ‘said the blessing’ reflects what a first-century reader would picture. The same verb is used in verses 50–53 for Jesus blessing the disciples and the disciples blessing God.

Most manuscripts, including the earliest, continue ‘and said to them, “Peace to you.”’ The SBLGNT follows a small group of ‘Western’ witnesses that lack the words, judging them to have been added from John 20:19; most modern translations include them. The same edition follows a similar shorter reading at verse 3, where most manuscripts have ‘the body of the Lord Jesus’.

The Greek word is pneuma, the ordinary word for ‘spirit’. Here and in verse 39 it means the disembodied spirit of a dead person, which is what ‘ghost’ means in modern English. Older versions have ‘spirit’; several recent ones have ‘ghost’.

notes.phrase: [And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.]
notes.note: The brackets reproduce those of the SBLGNT and mark the verse as doubtful. It is missing from a small group of ‘Western’ witnesses (one Greek manuscript and some early Latin and Syriac versions) and closely resembles John 20:20, which leads some scholars to regard it as a later addition. It is present in nearly all other manuscripts, including the earliest, and most modern editions and translations accept it.

The Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct; ‘repentance’ now tends to suggest mainly feeling sorry. Most translations keep ‘repentance’ as an established term understood to include a changed life. Some important manuscripts read ‘turning back for the forgiveness of sins’ in place of ‘and forgiveness’.

The Greek word here is the same one translated ‘Gentiles’ elsewhere in this translation; in the plural it can mean the non-Jewish peoples specifically or the peoples of the world generally. ‘Nations’ is used here because the scope is the whole world, starting from Jerusalem.

The brackets here and around ‘worshiped him and’ in verse 52 reproduce those of the SBLGNT and mark the words as doubtful. Both phrases are absent from a few ‘Western’ witnesses, and the first also from the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus. They are found in the great majority of manuscripts, including the earliest papyrus of Luke. Scholars are divided on whether they were added to make the ascension explicit or dropped to ease the comparison with Acts 1; most modern translations include them.

candidates.reason: The passive forms used of Jesus' resurrection can be rendered ‘was raised’ or ‘rose’, and the choice should be uniform across the Gospels, Acts and Paul.
The word ranges from bowing down before a superior to worship of God, and translators differ sharply on where to use ‘worship’ when Jesus is the object.
The λυτρ- word group (redeem, ransom, liberate) recurs in the Gospels, Paul, Hebrews and 1 Peter, and ‘redeem’ versus ‘set free’ needs one policy.
The same verb covers blessing God, blessing people and the blessing said over food, and translations vary between ‘bless’, ‘praise’ and ‘give thanks’.
Ancient units of distance recur in the Gospels and Revelation, and a single policy is needed on keeping the unit or converting to modern measures.
